title: Quadratics
overview: Quadratics underpin a huge share of Pure Maths 1 — from sketching parabolas to justifying whether an equation has real solutions. The key skills are solving quadratic equations by three different methods, and using the discriminant to reason about the number of roots without necessarily solving the equation.
syllabusPoints: carry out the process of completing the square for a quadratic polynomial and use this form to locate the vertex of the graph
find the discriminant of a quadratic polynomial and use it to determine the number of real roots
solve quadratic equations, and quadratic inequalities, in one variable
solve equations in x that are quadratic in some function of x

definitions.definition: The value b² − 4ac for a quadratic ax²+bx+c, which determines the number and type of roots without solving the equation.
Rewriting a quadratic ax²+bx+c in the form a(x+p)²+q, which directly reveals the turning point (−p, q).

sections.title: Solving quadratics (three methods)
content: Be fluent switching between three approaches depending on what the question wants: factorising (fastest, when it factorises nicely), the quadratic formula (always works), and completing the square (works, and reveals the turning point for free).

sections.title: Completing the square & the vertex
content: Write a(x+p)² + q. The graph's turning point is at (−p, q) — a minimum if a>0, maximum if a<0. This is the standard way to prove something is 'always positive' or find a minimum/maximum without calculus.

sections.title: The discriminant
content: For ax²+bx+c, the discriminant b²−4ac tells you the root type without solving: greater than 0 gives two distinct real roots, equal to 0 gives one repeated root (the graph touches the x-axis), and less than 0 gives no real roots (the graph doesn't cross the x-axis).

sections.title: Disguised quadratics
content: Some equations look unfamiliar but are quadratic in disguise — e.g. in terms of x², √x, or eˣ. Substitute u for the repeated expression, solve the quadratic in u, then convert back to x.

examples.label: Analysis chain
examples.content: x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0 → let u = x² → u²−5u+4=0 → u=1 or u=4 → x = ±1, ±2

examTips: 'Show that the equation has no real roots' wants the discriminant calculated AND explicitly compared to 0 in a sentence — a bare numeric answer without the comparison loses the conclusion mark.
When a question says 'hence' after asking you to complete the square, it's telling you to use that exact form for the next part (e.g. finding the minimum) — don't restart with the quadratic formula.
commonMistakes: Sign errors when completing the square — always double-check by expanding your answer back out.
Forgetting to convert back to x after solving a disguised quadratic in terms of u.
Stating 'no roots' when the discriminant is negative without explaining what that means graphically, when the question asks you to describe/explain.
quickRecall: Discriminant >0 → 2 roots, =0 → 1 repeated root, <0 → 0 real roots
Disguised quadratic → substitute u, solve, convert back
